name: Naloxone
summary: A competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression — the essential antidote for opioid overdose.
mechanism: Competitive antagonist at mu-opioid receptors, displacing opioids and reversing respiratory depression, sedation, and miosis; no intrinsic agonist activity.

dosing.adult: 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/SC, repeat every 2–3 min as needed; intranasal 2–4 mg; continuous infusion for long-acting opioids

safety.pregnancy: Use in overdose — reversal of maternal respiratory depression outweighs risk; may precipitate acute withdrawal in mother and fetus
warnings: Precipitated acute opioid withdrawal in dependent patients — agitation, vomiting, and autonomic storm can be severe
Half-life (20–90 min) is shorter than most opioids — renarcotization risk; observe and repeat doses
Rare pulmonary edema and cardiac arrhythmias, particularly with rapid reversal
High-potency opioids (fentanyl, buprenorphine) may need higher or repeated doses
monitoring: Respiratory status for at least 2 h after the last dose (longer for methadone/ER opioids)
Repeat dosing readiness and patient education on carry-narcan kits
safety.overdose: Essentially no intrinsic toxicity in the absence of opioids; effects wear off in 20–90 min, so repeated doses may be needed

clinicalPearls: Half-life (20–90 min) is shorter than most opioids — patients can renarcotize hours later; observe ≥2 h, longer after methadone or ER opioids
IV onset ~1–2 min vs ~2–5 min for IM/IN — community intranasal kits work with minimal training and save lives
good: Rapid reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression — the antidote that belongs in every overdose kit.
bad: As a diagnostic tool or beyond overdose reversal — its short duration invites renarcotization, and opioid-tolerant patients get precipitated withdrawal.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard neurology/pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
